item.title: Emulating absent land processes reduces carbon budgets in CMIP6 models
item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 24 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04111-9

Emulating missing land carbon-cycle processes across 11 CMIP6 models increases their estimated transient climate response to cumulative CO2 emissions, indicating a smaller carbon budget for the 2 °C climate target, as revealed by sensitivity tests based on UKESM.
item.dc:title: Emulating absent land processes reduces carbon budgets in CMIP6 models

item.title: Bay of Bengal cyclones fuel non-monsoon extreme precipitation on the central Tibetan Plateau
item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 24 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04154-y

Extreme precipitation events on the central Tibetan Plateau outside the monsoon season have been increasingly linked to cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and is projected to occur more frequently under global warming, as suggested by observations and model experiments.
item.dc:title: Bay of Bengal cyclones fuel non-monsoon extreme precipitation on the central Tibetan Plateau

item.title: In the synthetic biology era, engineered fungi could mitigate carbon dioxide emissions and enhance environmental resilience
item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 24 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04088-5

Soil fungi are an underexplored tool for climate mitigation, as discussed in this synthesis, which examines how synthetic biology could enhance their contributions to carbon sequestration as well as nutrient cycling, soil health, pollutant degradation, and ecosystem resilience.
item.dc:title: In the synthetic biology era, engineered fungi could mitigate carbon dioxide emissions and enhance environmental resilience
item.dc:creator: Kyle Davis
Joanna Tannous
